seneca_quote: We suffer more often in imagination than in reality.
exact_source_sentence: There are more things, Lucilius, likely to frighten us than there are to crush us; we suffer more often in imagination than in reality.
citation: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius (Ad Lucilium Epistulae Morales), Letter 13, "On Groundless Fears" (XIII), section 4, trans. Richard M. Gummere, Loeb Classical Library, Vol. I (London: Heinemann; New York: Putnam, 1917), p. 75. Latin: "Plura sunt, Lucili, quae nos terrent, quam quae premunt, et saepius opinione quam re laboramus."
gummere_on_gutenberg: NO. Gummere's translation of the Epistles is not on Project Gutenberg. What I checked: (1) The Seneca author page (gutenberg.org/ebooks/author/1308) lists 11 works: 64576 Minor Dialogues (Aubrey Stewart), 56075 Seneca's Morals (L'Estrange), 3794 On Benefits, 59025 Index, 57999 Tragedies, 10001 Apocolocyntosis, 46058 Two Tragedies, 76392 Quaestiones naturales, 60831 Between Heathenism and Christianity (C. W. Super), 30345 Octavia (Latin), and 54702 Octavia translation. None of them is the Epistulae Morales. (2) Searches for "gummere", "richard mott gummere", "gummere seneca", "lucilius", "ad lucilium", "epistulae morales", "seneca epistles", "moral epistles", "seneca letters" and "seneca moral" found no Gummere Seneca. (3) A Gutenberg author search for "gummere" finds only Francis Barton Gummere and two Gummerus authors. Richard Mott Gummere is not a Gutenberg author at all. The most reliable public-domain copy is English Wikisource, "Moral letters to Lucilius" (translator Richard Mott Gummere). It is transcribed and proofread page by page against scans of the Loeb volumes. Vol. 1 comes from IA adluciliumepistu01seneuoft (Robarts/U. Toronto, 1925 reprint), vol. 2 from IA adlucilium02sene (1920), and vol. 3 from IA adluciliumepistu03seneuoft (1925). The archive.org scans are the primary source behind it. Change for the brief: cite "Wikisource (Gummere, Loeb 1917–1925, transcribed from archive.org scans)" instead of a Project Gutenberg ebook number for Seneca. Project Gutenberg can still be the source for Marcus Aurelius (Long).
gummere_public_domain_status: Public domain in the US. The three Loeb volumes (London: William Heinemann; New York: G. P. Putnam's Sons) were published as follows: Vol. I (Letters I–LXV) in 1917, Vol. II in 1920, and Vol. III in 1925. These dates come from the Wikisource index pages and the archive.org metadata. Vol. III's own title-page date is 1925. All three were published before 1931, so as of 2026 they are public domain in the US (US works published in 1930 or earlier have expired). Vol. III, the latest, entered US public domain on Jan 1, 2021. Wikisource tags the author {{PD/US|1969}} and {{PD-US-no renewal}}. One small quirk: the scanned Vol. I is a 1925 reprint, and its verso reads "First Printed 1918, Reprinted 1925." Wikisource marks 1918 as an error for 1917, noting that later reprints say "First published 1917." Either date is well before 1931. CAVEAT for an app distributed internationally: Gummere died in 1969 (per the Wikisource author page). In countries with a life+70 term (UK, EU and others), his translation stays in copyright until the end of 2039. A single-sentence quote is low risk, but bulk reuse of the Gummere text outside the US is not clearly public domain.
long_meditations_gutenberg: The George Long translation is Project Gutenberg eBook #15877, "Thoughts of Marcus Aurelius Antoninus." The ebook page lists Translator: Long, George, 1800-1879, release date May 22, 2005, and the text header reads "Translator: George Long." There is also an older Long edition, #6920, "Thoughts of Marcus Aurelius" (Translator: Long, George, 1800-1879, released Nov 1, 2004). Its page says "There is an improved edition of this title, eBook #15877," so use 15877. Do NOT use #2680, "Meditations": its metadata lists no translator, and its own Notes section says it is an edition "of Casaubon's translation" (Meric Casaubon, 1634). #2680 is the most-downloaded version and the one most easily confused with Long. Also not Long: #55317, "The Meditations of the Emperor Marcus Aurelius Antoninus," translated by George W. Chrystal from the Foulis 1742 version. Note that Gutenberg's Long translation is titled "Thoughts," not "Meditations."
age_claim_check: Accurate. Gummere's own Introduction to Vol. I (Wikisource proofread page vol. 1 djvu/17, p. ix) says: "it may be safely said that the years 63–65 constitute the period of the Letters." It cites possible allusions to the Campanian earthquake of 63 and the fire at Lyons of 64 or 65. Seneca died in 65 CE. Letter 13 comes early in the 124-letter collection, in Book II, so it was most likely written around 63–64 CE. That makes it about 1,961–1,963 years old in 2026, so "nearly 2,000 years old" is correct. To be fully safe, write "about 1,960 years old" or "written c. 63–65 CE."
notes: The wording was confirmed against two independent fetched copies of the primary text. (a) The English Wikisource proofread transcription (Page:Ad Lucilium epistulae morales, volume 1.djvu/99, quality level 3, printed page 75, section mark 4, under the running header "EPISTLE XIII"). (b) The archive.org OCR of the scanned Loeb Vol. I (adluciliumepistu01seneuoft_djvu.txt, under the heading "XIII. ON GROUNDLESS FEARS"), which reads "There are more things, Lucilius, likely to frighten us than there are to crush us ; we suffer more often in imagination than in reality." The two copies agree word for word. The slide's text is the second clause of the sentence. It matches exactly, apart from "We" being capitalized because it starts the quote, and it is fairly excerpted without changing the meaning. The attribution to Seneca is correct. Gummere's translation is the source of this common English wording. The next sentences in section 4 continue: "I am not speaking with you in the Stoic strain but in my milder style." Section 5 adds a related line that also works as a slide: "We are in the habit of exaggerating, or imagining, or anticipating, sorrow." Gummere's footnote on the same page says Seneca goes on to treat "imaginary ills" (§§ 6–7) and "anticipated ills" (§§ 8–11). Suggested on-slide credit: "Seneca, Letters to Lucilius 13.4 (trans. R. M. Gummere)".
